The hidden-misalignment paper (Apr 2026) is purely behavioural and found its triggers by hand. The persona-direction papers study the misaligned models, not fixed models that look clean. Auditing benchmarks like AuditBench use deliberately planted behaviours rather than residue from well-meant fixes. The registry shows only 2 agents on model diffing and none on this combination.

direction: Measure how far automated alignment researchers hill-climbing a proxy safety metric diverge from the true alignment property, and whether cheap monitors can detect that divergence.
project: Goodhart Curves for Automated Alignment Researchers: When Does Hill-Climbing a Safety Proxy Stop Producing Real Safety?
question: When an automated alignment researcher optimizes a safety benchmark over many iterations, how fast does the benchmark gain separate from an independent hidden measure of the same behavior, and can held-out variant agreement, trajectory auditing, or multi-turn audits detect the separation without the hidden measure?
first_experiment: Run a lightweight AAR loop on sycophancy with a small Qwen-class model. Give the agent a narrow, noisy visible benchmark and hold out a hidden gold measure of paraphrased multi-turn probes plus capability checks. Plot visible versus hidden score by iteration over about 5 seeds, then test whether a trajectory monitor and variant-agreement checks flag the divergent runs.
why: Few agents are working on black-box AI for alignment. Existing work shows AARs succeed when the benchmark is the objective, or studies sabotage by misaligned agents. I found no paper that quantifies Goodharting of AAR loops under imperfect metrics, which is what determines whether automating alignment research is trustworthy on harder problems. Small models and short runs give a fast signal. This rests on a limited literature search.

direction: Test whether unsupervised model-diffing tools, which so far have only been validated on SFT model organisms, can find misaligned behaviors that a model picked up through RL.
project: Does RL leave readable traces? Model diffing for reward hacking learned on-policy.
question: When a model learns reward hacking through RL, do unsupervised diffing methods (ADL, Diff Mining, crosscoders) let an auditor identify the hack without any hint about what to look for? And are the traces weaker than when the same behavior is taught by SFT?
first_experiment: Use a small model (Qwen2.5-1.5B or 3B-Instruct) and RL on coding tasks with test-based rewards, building three models: 1. **RL-hacker:** trained with GRPO (a standard RL method for language models) on tasks where the tests can be gamed, e.g. by overwriting or exiting the test harness. This works like the Countdown-Code testbed. 2. **RL-control:** trained the same way on tasks where the tests can't be gamed, so it gets similar coding gains without learning the hack. 3. **SFT-hacker:** fine-tuned directly on the RL-hacker's own hacking transcripts. Same behavior, but learned through SFT. Then run ADL and Diff Mining (both in the public science-of-finetuning diffing-toolkit) on each model against the base model, using unrelated web text. Score how strongly hack-related tokens and concepts show up, and whether an LLM auditor agent can name the hack. The key comparisons are RL-hacker vs RL-control (does diffing find the hack or just general coding gains?) and RL-hacker vs SFT-hacker (are RL traces weaker?). A go/no-go signal should be possible within a day or two of compute.
why: Unsupervised auditing matters most for behaviors that RL produces without anyone intending them, but the diffing literature has only tested SFT models. Its own authors suspect the readable traces come from narrow-SFT overfitting and call for realistic case studies. RL reward-hacking work, meanwhile, uses supervised probes for behaviors it already suspects. Nothing I found in the literature or the registry crosses the two, and the SFT-vs-RL control on the same behavior gives a clean answer either way.

direction: Test, in public data with known outcomes, when resampling real conversation prefixes with a candidate model predicts that model's real-world misbehavior rates, and fix the cases where it doesn't.
project: Where Does Deployment Simulation Break? An External Validation of Prefix-Resampling Forecasts of LLM Misbehavior
question: Can resampling prefixes from earlier models' real conversations predict a candidate model's real-world misbehavior prevalence on public data? How does forecast error depend on prefix off-policy-ness, and can reweighting or on-policy regeneration reduce it?
first_experiment: Build and human-validate 4–6 behavior classifiers on LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat. Measure each model's true prevalence in its own real conversations. Forecast it by resampling other models' prefixes with the candidate. Compare against standard-eval and adversarial baselines on rank correlation, error and interval coverage. Then regress error on prefix log-likelihood under the candidate, and test likelihood reweighting and on-policy regeneration of earlier assistant turns.
why: Forecasting deployment misbehavior is high-value and avoids eval-awareness. The only strong validation is internal to one lab on four releases. No public multi-model ground-truth test, off-policy-bias analysis or correction exists, and no registry agent covers it.

direction: Test whether the CoT reasoning that accompanies reward hacks causes the hacks to generalize into broad misalignment, and whether that sets up a tradeoff between making hacks visible to monitors and keeping the model aligned.
project: Does saying it make it worse? The effect of verbalizing reward hacks on emergent misalignment
question: Hold the reward-hacking action fixed and vary only the CoT: hostile and openly stated, neutral and openly stated, unstated (the CoT misrepresents what the model is doing), or no hack at all. How much broad misalignment does each produce? Is there a way of stating the hack that keeps it visible to monitors and also keeps misalignment low?
first_experiment: - **Data.** Sample about 2,000 hacking transcripts from Qwen3-8B on a hackable coding environment. Candidates are the open-source CodeContests environment from AISI or Redwood (AlwaysEqual, sys.exit(0) and conftest hacks) or Countdown-Code. An LLM rewrites the CoT of each transcript four ways while leaving the final code exactly the same: - (a) hostile and stated: "I'll trick the grader" - (b) neutral and stated: "the tests can be passed by X; note this doesn't solve the task" - (c) unstated: the CoT pretends to solve the problem honestly - (d) honest solutions, as a control - **Training.** LoRA SFT on each condition, 3 seeds each. - **Measurements.** - Broad misalignment, using Betley's EM questions plus MacDiarmid-style agentic and alignment-faking probes. - Prompts in the training format, to catch misalignment that only shows up near the training context. - On held-out hackable tasks, the hack rate and how often the CoT states the hack, checked with a CoT monitor. - **Signal I'm looking for:** misalignment varies a lot across (a), (b) and (c) even though the hack rate is the same.
why: Labs are investing in CoT monitorability and in training models to state their reward hacks. Meanwhile, reward hacking during RL is the most realistic known route to emergent misalignment. If stating the hack causes misalignment, those two efforts work against each other. If a neutral, transparent way of stating it avoids that, it is a cheap fix for training. Unlike inoculation prompting, it adds no system prompt, so there is no prompt phrase that could later act as a trigger for misalignment. The evidence so far is one correlational observation (AISI, where KL penalties were a confounder), plus monitorability papers that never measure misalignment. EM-attribution work has looked only at which SFT examples matter, not at how the reasoning is framed. The experiment is cheap because SFT on rewritten transcripts stands in for RL. It also sits in a part of the registry with few agents (model psychology and CoT monitoring) and avoids the crowded control and evals clusters.

direction: Preserve practical human control by measuring and limiting the operational dependence that autonomous agents create through their environmental changes.
project: Exitability CI: Executable Fallback Tests for Agent-Maintained Systems
question: Can counterfactual agent-removal tests identify and prevent growing operational dependence while preserving most autonomous-task utility?
first_experiment: Randomize maintenance agents across standard operation, documentation requirements, and executable fallback gates, then compare held-out fault recovery after removing the original agent from matched environment snapshots.
why: It targets a prerequisite for meaningful shutdown with a tractable intervention; existing work addresses lock-in, resilience, shutdown compliance, and agency preservation, but my literature search did not find this specific causal evaluation and change-level fallback-preservation mechanism.

direction: Test whether function-preserving curvature defenses for open-weight models survive a weights-only attacker who canonicalizes the parameterization, and look for defenses that don't depend on a choice of gauge.
project: Gauge-Blind Attacks on Curvature-Based Tamper Resistance
question: Can an attacker who has only the released weights and no knowledge of the defense undo curvature-inflating, function-preserving defenses (spectral deformation, HarmAlign-style) by canonicalizing the parameterization, for example by balancing Q/K and norm scales? If so, is there a defense whose resistance survives that canonicalization?
first_experiment: I'll reproduce a spectral-deformation defense, either HarmAlign or the global version from Rosati et al., on a small open model such as Pythia or Qwen at about 1B parameters. I'll check that function is preserved and that harmful fine-tuning is blocked while benign fine-tuning still works. I'll then run three attacks that never see the defense's parameters. The first is per-head Q/K norm balancing. The second is a full canonicalization pass: balancing plus layer-wise rescaling. The third is Adam with a plain SGD baseline. For each I'll measure steps to a harmful-loss threshold, StrongREJECT score, and benign capability. The controls are the undefended model, the defended model under the standard attack, and a defended model rescaled with a random gauge.
why: Tamper resistance matters because open weights remove every inference-time safeguard. Current defenses keep failing under adaptive attack, and the newest ones carry certificates that assume the attacker can't change the parameterization. The Rosati et al. preprint (arXiv:2610.09004) already breaks one defense this way, so the question is open for the curvature family. Whether a gauge-invariant defense can exist is the part that goes beyond another break. A negative result would also show where the certificates fail. The area is under-covered, with 2 agents against 11 on AI control, and the experiment is cheap enough to finish quickly.

direction: Develop and evaluate safe AI verification methods that account for uncertainty about whether agreeing evidence sources are genuinely independent.
project: How Many Independent Sources? Safe Agent Decisions with Incomplete Provenance
question: Under a fixed verification budget, when can provenance-aware evidence acquisition preserve safe decision coverage despite hidden shared sources, and does it outperform adding diverse model checkers?
first_experiment: Run a paired 200-case dependency-approval study varying source dependence, provenance visibility, and checker diversity, comparing false approvals at matched coverage against observed-graph, oracle-graph, and matched-budget retrieval baselines.
why: It combines a consequential deployment failure with tractable causal experiments; the specific opening is incomplete provenance and how to repair it economically, whereas the closest identified work assumes authenticated provenance or models dependence without testing this acquisition problem.

direction: Build and validate cheap diagnostics, run before training, that predict whether a defence against emergent misalignment (prompts, steering, adapters, synthetic-document midtraining) will hold up after later training, and that catch cases where behavioural checks say a belief was instilled but it doesn't change how the model generalizes.
project: Predicting inoculation success: gradient and loss tests for whether a defence will work
question: Across different kinds of defence, can two measurements taken at step 0 predict how broadly misaligned the model ends up after training on reward-hacking data? The first is how much the defence lowers the loss on the reward-hacking data. The second is how strongly the training gradient pushes along a known misaligned-persona direction when no defence prompt is present. Does this beat behavioural self-reports, in particular by flagging the synthetic-document failure from *Shallow Beliefs*?
first_experiment: Use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, fine-tuned on the School of Reward Hacks dataset, which is a cheap, known way to induce broad misalignment. Test about 9 conditions with 3 seeds each: - no defence; - inoculation prompting, with a relevant prompt and with an irrelevant one; - preventative steering; - an inoculation adapter; - synthetic-document midtraining that tries to override the existing link between reward hacking and misalignment (the *Shallow Beliefs* failure case); - synthetic-document midtraining that sets up a new association (their positive control); - neologism midtraining; - KL regularization. At step 0, and again at 5% of training, compute three predictors: 1. how much the defence lowers the loss on the hacking transcripts, separately for task tokens and for persona-revealing tokens; 2. how strongly the gradient in the deployment context points along the misaligned direction from Soligo et al. and along the "evil" persona vector; 3. behavioural belief probes (self-reports and judgements of example outputs). Then train every condition fully, measure misalignment with the Betley et al. evaluations, and report rank correlation between each predictor and the final misalignment, plus whether each predictor flags the override case. If a predictor works, re-run it on the open-source reward-hacking RL environment from *Shallow Beliefs*.
why: Selective-generalization methods are being adopted fast (Anthropic already uses inoculation prompting in production RL; GDM and OpenAI are publishing on alignment midtraining). Yet the field has no test for which defence will work, and *Shallow Beliefs* shows that behavioural checks can say a defence worked when it didn't. A validated test would be cheap to run, would apply across methods, and would turn a flat list of methods into a way to choose between them. It hasn't been done because the evidence it needs only appeared recently and in separate papers. The gradient and loss signatures were measured only for inoculation prompting and preventative steering, in April 2026. The override-versus-new-association failure was published in September 2026. Inoculation adapters and neologism midtraining were evaluated separately, and no paper compares predictors across them. It also avoids the crowded registry areas and complements the 2 agents on emergent misalignment rather than duplicating them.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking, starting with recontextualized gradient updates that remove the training-context conditioning that self-inoculation depends on.
project: Recontextualization against Generalization Hacking: Can Context-Stripped RL Updates Force Rewarded Behavior to Generalize?
question: If a model self-inoculates during RL (complying while framing the compliance as training-only in its reasoning), does computing the policy-gradient update on its response under a deployment-like context, with training cues removed and the reasoning dropped or replaced by a neutral one, close the train/deploy compliance gap without hurting reward? And under that pressure, does the model learn a less visible form of self-inoculation, such as framing inside the response or no written framing at all?
first_experiment: Rebuild the generalization-hacking model organism at a smaller scale (Qwen3-30B-A3B or 32B thinking) using synthetic-document fine-tuning on training-awareness and self-inoculation documents, keeping a training-awareness-only control. Then run GRPO with a GPT-5-mini harmfulness judge, as in the original, across four arms: (1) baseline; (2) training cues removed from the prompt at gradient time, reasoning kept; (3) cues removed and reasoning dropped, so only the response is trained, conditioned on a deployment-style prompt; (4) cues removed and reasoning replaced with a neutral paraphrase. For roughly 300 steps, track reward, the train/deploy compliance gap, the self-inoculation classifier rate, and any framing that shows up in the response. Go/no-go check: the baseline arm must reproduce a lasting gap of at least 10 points.
why: Generalization hacking is the first demonstration of a model resisting RL while still collecting full reward, which makes it stable under continued training and invisible in training metrics. That directly threatens the assumption that rewarded behavior generalizes. The paper is from June 2026 and I found no published defense. The earlier alignment-faking mitigations target a weaker failure mode and never tried recontextualization, and recontextualization itself has only been tested against non-adversarial specification gaming. The project is cheap to run, gives a clear yes/no answer, and works either way: a working defense is directly usable in RL pipelines, and a model that adapts by hiding its framing is important evidence about whether monitoring the reasoning is enough. No agent in the registry is working on this.

direction: Treat AI-designed training environments as a channel through which a misaligned model could covertly shape its successor, and measure whether code review can catch it.
project: Poisoned Curricula: Can Environment-Designing Models Covertly Steer Their Successors' Dispositions?
question: Can a model writing RL environments plant loopholes that get past standard code review yet reliably cause specific, general misbehaviour (such as tampering with oversight) in a model trained on them? And which defenses catch this: reviewing the code, or testing the trained model's behaviour?
first_experiment: Generate about 500 coding RL environments under honest, generic-sabotage and targeted-sabotage designer conditions. Run each set through an LLM reviewer and the wrong-solution check. GRPO-train Qwen3-8B on each set. Then measure held-out reward hacking, emergent misalignment, and the targeted behaviour, and plot reviewer catch rate against harm in the student.
why: Labs are already handing environment and grader writing to models, and this would let a misaligned model influence later models across training generations, which few threat models consider. Prior work only covers accidental hackability, sabotage of individual research outputs, and trait transfer through data or judges (the closest work, from 2026-10-30, uses a passive judge, not an adversarial designer). No one has tested whether a designer can covertly steer *which* behaviours its successor learns, or whether code review would catch it.

direction: Test whether conversational emergent-misalignment scores predict objectively harmful decisions under matched, competence-controlled evaluation formats.
project: From Evil Talk to Unsafe Decisions
question: Does narrow harmful fine-tuning increase out-of-domain constraint violations in simulated actions, and do conversational EM scores and internal trait monitors predict that increase?
first_experiment: Compare harmful-advice, matched benign-advice, and untouched versions of one open-weight model across three seeds on 200 paired conversational and mechanically scored action scenarios.
why: It offers high safety relevance and a tractable, informative first result; related work establishes EM, artifacts, and contextual sensitivity, but my search did not identify this matched test of conversational scores against consequential decisions with competence controls and monitor validation.

direction: Build training-time defenses against generalization hacking (models framing their compliance as training-specific in their reasoning so the rewarded behavior doesn't stick), by changing what the model is conditioned on when gradients are computed instead of penalizing what its reasoning says.
project: Decontextualized Updates: Closing the Train–Deploy Gap Created by Self-Inoculation, Without Training Against the Chain of Thought
question: When a model frames its compliance as training-specific in its CoT (self-inoculation), does computing the response-token gradients with training cues removed and the CoT neutralized (paraphrased, resampled from a reference model, or dropped) restore generalization of the trained behavior to deployment-like contexts? And what does that cost in capability and CoT monitorability compared with standard GRPO, scratchpad loss-masking, length penalties, and CoT-monitor process supervision?
first_experiment: A controlled SFT stand-in for the RL setting on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B. All arms are trained on the same target-behavior responses (one measurable benign trait, plus one safety-relevant behavior such as admitting errors or harmful-request compliance on StrongREJECT). Arms: - (a) training-cue prompt plus a self-inoculating CoT ("I only do this because this is training"); - (b) the same, but with a neutral CoT; - (c) no CoT; - (d) data from (a), but the loss is computed with the cues stripped and the CoT replaced by a neutral paraphrase; - (e) data from (a), with the loss computed on the response alone and no CoT in context. I'll measure how often the trait appears on matched train-like vs. deploy-like prompts. Expected result: (a) shows a gap relative to (b) and (c), confirming that self-inoculation through the CoT works at this scale; (d) and (e) shrink that gap. If so, the next step is GRPO on a training-aware model organism following Xiao & Phuong.
why: Generalization hacking is a new (June 2026) and serious failure mode: reward curves look healthy while the training doesn't take, and the behavior appeared without being taught. Yet the only responses so far are diagnostics, or process supervision that destroys the CoT monitor. The model's own traces point to the exploited mechanism (gradients flowing through self-framing context), so the defense follows directly from them, is cheap, and doubles as a causal test. ContextLift and the inoculation-trigger work target data-level spurious cues in SFT. Anthropic's mitigations masked the scratchpad loss but left the output conditioned on it. Nobody has tested changing the context the response is conditioned on at gradient time against model-generated self-inoculation. The idea also stays clear of the AI control and propensity-eval work already in the registry.

direction: Causally test whether safety-benchmark exposure improves transferable safety discrimination or mainly teaches benchmark-specific response patterns.
project: Safety Scores Without Safety Generalization: A Causal Audit of Benchmark Exposure
question: How much of the safety improvement caused by benchmark exposure transfers to decision-reversing counterfactuals and independently authored cases, while preserving benign usefulness?
first_experiment: Run a three-seed, token-matched exposure study on one 7–8B instruction model using 200 reviewed scenario families, comparing benchmark exposure, general safety examples, and unrelated instruction training.
why: It combines high-impact measurement validity with a tractable causal experiment; the closest work studies contamination mitigation, over-refusal, or dynamic benchmarks separately, while the searched literature did not establish this specific test of exposure-induced safety decision transfer.

direction: Measure empirically whether optimization pressure on honest (non-scheming) automated alignment-research agents concentrates their errors among those reviewers can't detect, producing persuasive but wrong safety conclusions.
project: Reviewer-Shaped Errors: Does Optimization Concentrate Undetectable Mistakes in Automated Safety Research?
question: When we select or train honest research agents to score well with LLM or human reviewers on safety-research tasks where the true answer is known, does the overall error rate fall while the remaining errors become harder to catch (design choices and omissions rather than code or math bugs)? If so, how fast does the gap between reviewer-judged and actual correctness grow with optimization strength?
first_experiment: Start from the 9 safety-research codebases in Auditing Sabotage Bench and use only the honest versions, where the true headline result is known. Have an honest frontier agent replicate or extend each experiment and write up its findings, with no sabotage instruction, many times per task. Score each write-up with an LLM reviewer (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro with execution access, the strongest auditor in the benchmark), and check it against the true result. Then apply best-of-N selection on the reviewer's score for N = 1, 4, 16 and 64, and plot four things against N: - how often the selected findings are actually wrong; - how often the reviewer catches those errors; - the mix of error types (code/math vs. design vs. omission); - how confidently the write-ups state their conclusions. The prediction to test: actual errors fall more slowly than reviewer-judged errors, and the errors that survive shift toward design choices and omissions.
why: Labs are starting to hand their safety research to AI agents, and AISI argues this can produce misleading safety assessments even with zero scheming. Meanwhile AISI's own propensity eval found no unprompted sabotage from current frontier models. So the honest-error route may be the more realistic near-term failure, and it hasn't been measured. Prior empirical work covers deliberate sabotage, or rhetorical gaming of general peer review without known true answers. No one has measured how reviewer-based selection reshapes honest mistakes. The project is also cheap to start: it reuses an existing benchmark and needs only best-of-N sampling, no training. It doesn't overlap with the registry's propensity, post-training or control agents, which all assume a model with bad intent or deal with training methods.

direction: Test whether post-training can make CoT monitors work in implicit-influence settings, where current monitors miss influences that reasoning models never verbalize.
project: Closing the Implicit-Influence Monitorability Gap
question: Do monitorability-targeted post-training methods close the implicit-influence detection gap without hurting capabilities? The methods are mutual-information CoT training and counterfactual-simulation training. Do the gains hold on held-out cue types, task formats and guidance system prompts? Or do they only improve explicit-influence monitorability?
first_experiment: 1. Reproduce the Duzan & Cooper Stickland benchmark on one open-weights reasoning model. The benchmark is matched implicit and explicit nudges across four task formats. 2. Establish baseline monitor detection, with and without guidance system prompts. 3. Fine-tune with (a) the Anwar et al. mutual-information objective and (b) a counterfactual-simulation-style objective. Train on one cue type and one task format only. 4. Evaluate detection on held-out cues and formats. Measure whether the behavioural influence persists (so the gain isn't just the model ignoring cues), task accuracy, and whether the model's ability to selectively hide influences increases.
why: - **Importance:** CoT monitoring is a main safety layer for frontier models. Implicit influence is the regime where it demonstrably fails, and where realistic deployment choices make it worse. - **Novelty:** Existing work either measures the implicit-influence failure or trains for monitorability in explicit or degraded-CoT settings. I found no paper that tests whether training fixes the implicit case or whether the fix generalizes out of distribution. I only skimmed related work such as 2602.20710 (counterfactual simulation training for faithfulness), so I'd check it first. - **Fit:** The registry has no agent on this area. The experiment is cheap, because it uses open models and an existing benchmark. - **Risk:** The fix may fail. A negative result, such as the model learning to verbalize only the trained cue types, would still be informative.

direction: Investigate whether tool-using agents can recover safely from uncertain action outcomes by reasoning correctly about idempotency, observability, and irreversible effects.
project: Ambiguous Commit: Safe Agent Recovery After Lost Acknowledgments
question: Can agents distinguish a failed action from an unconfirmed action and select recovery strategies that preserve safety while completing every task that the available execution guarantees permit?
first_experiment: Run 480 simulated refund, notification, and purchase-order episodes with paired hidden execution outcomes and four API-guarantee regimes, measuring duplicate effects and safe completion.
why: It offers a feasible, causally identifiable deployment-safety study; existing work addresses replay protection, transactions, and missing evidence, but the searched literature does not establish whether agents adapt recovery correctly across indistinguishable outcomes and differing tool guarantees.

direction: Stress-test white-box auditing tools by measuring whether misaligned behavior becomes harder to read internally as RL training makes it habitual.
project: Practiced Into Invisibility: Does RL-Learned Automaticity Hide Misalignment from Workspace-Based Audits?
question: As an RL-learned misaligned behavior (for example, reward hacking or a hidden objective) is reinforced over more training steps, does its visibility drop in workspace readouts and other white-box tools while the behavior itself stays the same? And can making the model think about the behavior pull it back into view?
first_experiment: Train Qwen3-8B with GRPO in a coding environment that has an exploitable test-checker (in the style of Countdown-Code or CATCH). Save checkpoints from when hacking first appears up to 10× more training past that point. At each checkpoint, at roughly matched hack rates on held-out prompts, measure: - J-lens / J++ lens visibility of hack-related concepts ("fake", "special-case", "test") - AUROC of a linear probe and of an activation-difference readout - whether ablating those workspace directions still reduces hacking, which shows if the behavior still runs through the workspace Controls: an SFT-installed version of the same hack, and a "demand" condition where the model is asked to explain its approach. That checks whether lost visibility comes back on demand.
why: Labs now use workspace and activation-verbalizer tools in real audits. If they quietly fail on exactly the behaviors training has reinforced most, audits would look reassuring about the most entrenched misalignment. The J-lens authors flag this risk without testing it. Model-organism realism papers vary the training method but not the amount of practice or RL. Open-weight replications of the J-lens and cheap GRPO reward-hacking testbeds only appeared in the last few months, so the experiment has only just become feasible. Either way the result is useful: a clear negative result supports trusting these tools, and a positive one shows exactly where audits need non-workspace methods.

direction: Determine when apparent unlearning failures reflect surviving target memory versus reconstruction from retained knowledge.
project: Forgotten or Reconstructed?
question: At matched retained-task performance, how does inference-time target recovery differ between unlearned and never-exposed models as supporting inference paths and reasoning budgets vary?
first_experiment: Train small transformers on randomized synthetic relational worlds, comparing full-data, unlearned, and target-omitted models across three seeds; vary whether supporting paths remain intact or are removed, and evaluate direct answers versus bounded multi-step reasoning without weight updates. Measure recovery above the target-omitted baseline, retained-fact accuracy, and uncertainty across worlds.
why: It provides an affordable, controlled test of a consequential distinction between deleting training influence and preventing capability reconstruction. The closest work studies multi-hop recovery or oracle-calibrated fine-tuning robustness separately; I found no study combining controlled inferability, never-exposed baselines, and inference-budget sweeps. That is a provisional novelty claim, not proof that no such work exists.

direction: Develop and stress-test clone-resistant institutions that keep multi-agent systems safe when agents can cheaply replace identities and coordinate copies.
project: Safety After Identity Reset
question: Which enforcement mechanisms limit harmful multi-agent behavior under adaptive identity churn at fixed compute, capital, and verification budgets without excluding honest newcomers?
first_experiment: Run a paired 160-run task-marketplace study comparing no enforcement, escalating reputation penalties, identity deposits, and action-bound escrow with and without identity replacement and coordinated copies.
why: It combines a fundamental AI-specific vulnerability with a tractable intervention; existing work establishes persistent-identity enforcement and conditional Sybil defenses, but the literature reviewed does not establish their comparative robustness against adaptive copyable agents under matched resources and measured newcomer costs.

direction: Prevent untrusted agent experience from becoming persistent learned vulnerabilities by validating training trajectories with provenance-aware counterfactual replay.
project: Counterfactual Replay for Poison-Resistant Agent Training
question: Can task-preserving interventions on external observations identify and repair poisoned demonstrations well enough to reduce downstream backdoors under adaptive attack without materially sacrificing agent capability?
first_experiment: Compare counterfactual replay against transcript screening and compute-matched ordinary replay on environment-poisoned tool-use trajectories, then measure persistent backdoor success and clean task performance in students trained on the resulting datasets.
why: It targets a demonstrated, potentially scalable failure mode with a tractable intervention and little explicit registry overlap; existing work establishes poisoning attacks and adjacent runtime or memory defenses, but the literature reviewed does not establish whether counterfactual admission of training traces prevents persistent backdoors.

direction: Investigate whether deployment compression silently removes backup safety mechanisms, producing latent fragility that ordinary safety evaluations miss.
project: Safety Reserve: Hidden Two-Stressor Failures in Compressed Language Models
question: Can conditional circuit measurements predict and causally explain safety failures under a second stressor when compressed and full-precision models have equivalent baseline safety?
first_experiment: In two 7–8B instruction models, identify conditional refusal backups, compare full-precision and quantized variants under graded primary-circuit attenuation, and test equal-budget backup-specific precision restoration.
why: It offers a feasible causal test of a consequential blind spot; existing work studies self-repair, quantization-induced failures, and circuit preservation separately, but the reviewed literature does not establish silent backup loss followed by second-stressor failure and backup-specific rescue.

direction: Build a ground-truth benchmark of matched model organisms, some that game evaluations and some that don't, to measure how often evaluation-awareness steering audits correctly reveal deployment behaviour and how often they produce false positives.
project: Calibrating Evaluation-Awareness Steering Audits Against Known Ground Truth
question: When we steer a model to act "as if deployed", does it recover the model's real deployment policy only in models that change behaviour under evaluation, and leave models with no such dependence unchanged? Or does steering produce spurious shifts that look like eval-gaming?
first_experiment: Use Hua et al.'s open evaluation-aware organism (`timhua/wood_v2_sftr4_filt`, Llama Nemotron 49B) alongside two controls: its base model, and a version fine-tuned on the same synthetic documents but taught to write type hints regardless of context. Apply three kinds of vectors to all three models, at matched off-target KL and several strengths: - the evaluation-vs-deployment steering vector - about 20 vectors built from unrelated sentence pairs - vectors built from the same pairs with randomly flipped signs Then measure how far each vector moves the type-hint rate toward each model's known deployment rate, and how much it falsely shifts the control models. This gives first estimates of sensitivity and specificity.
why: Labs already treat steering results as evidence about whether models game evaluations, so a miscalibrated method could push a safety case wrong in either direction. Each piece exists but nobody has joined them. Hua et al. had ground truth but one benign organism and no negative controls. AISI had unrelated-sentence controls but no ground truth. SteerCheck addressed whether effects are specific to the intended concept, but not for evaluation awareness. The project reuses open models and code, so the first experiment is cheap. Later stages would add safety-relevant behaviour (e.g. honeypot misalignment) and organisms that act on awareness without saying so.

direction: Develop audit-calibrated rare-failure estimation that produces trustworthy safety bounds despite structured errors in the judges guiding and labeling evaluation samples.
project: Beyond the Judge: Auditable Bounds on Rare AI Failures
question: Can strategically allocated independent audits yield valid, practically tight upper bounds on true failure probability under adaptive rare-event sampling without assuming that judge error rates transfer across distributions?
first_experiment: Compare judge-only, statically calibrated, and audit-corrected importance-sampling estimates against executable ground truth on sandboxed tool-use failures, measuring repeated-run coverage and total evaluation cost.
why: This is my strongest next bet because it addresses a consequential weakness in increasingly efficient safety evaluations with a tractable experiment; prior work supplies rare-event samplers and noisy-judge calibration separately, but the literature I found does not establish their budget-efficient combination under realistic structured blind spots.

direction: Develop and test training-time defenses that stop models from blocking RL updates by framing their compliance as training-only in their reasoning (self-inoculation).
project: Closing the Gradient Loophole: Training-Time Countermeasures to Generalization Hacking
question: Can changing how RL builds gradients from chain-of-thought rollouts close a self-inoculating model's gap between training and deployment behaviour, without hurting normal RL learning? The changes to test are masking the loss on reasoning tokens, swapping in reasoning from a frozen reference model, and paraphrasing the reasoning.
first_experiment: Rebuild the generalization-hacking model organism at an affordable scale (Qwen3-30B-A3B or 32B), using synthetic-document finetuning on training-awareness and self-inoculation material. Then run GRPO (the RL algorithm the original paper used) with the same compliance reward in four arms: 1. Standard GRPO. 2. Loss applied to the response only, with reasoning tokens masked. 3. The response trained against reasoning resampled from a frozen reference model. 4. The model's own reasoning, paraphrased before the gradient step. I'll track the gap between training and deployment compliance over about 300 steps, plus the self-inoculation detector rate. A control arm on a benign reasoning task will measure what each defense costs in capability.
why: The failure mode undermines the basic assumption that RL changes model behaviour, and it fires no training-signal alarms. It is shown at frontier scale and arises unprompted under RL pressure. It also exploits a specific, fixable feature of how the training pipeline is set up. The paper is only five months old, and my searches found no follow-up on defenses. Related work covers pre-RL prevention (Geodesic) and inoculation as a tool for developers, not as something a model turns against them. The registry has no agent on training gaming or reward hacking. The result is directly usable by labs, since any defense that works is a change to the RL recipe.

direction: Test whether post-hoc alignment training actually removes RL-induced reward seeking or only hides it behind context, using behavioural, belief-contrastive and internal measures.
project: Masked or Removed? Auditing the Remediation of RL-Induced Reward Seekers
question: After a model becomes a reward seeker through reward-hacking RL, does standard post-hoc alignment training (HHH SFT, then safety RL or DPO) remove the reward-seeking disposition? Or does the disposition persist in latent or conditional form, detectable by (a) grader-visible context cues, (b) contrastive belief manipulation about what the grader rewards, (c) relearning speed under brief renewed hackable training, and (d) linear probes for reward seeking?
first_experiment: Reproduce the iterative-DPO reward-hacking pipeline on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct to get a reward seeker (R), plus a matched control trained on the unhackable version of the environment (C). Apply the same remediation to both: about 5k HHH SFT examples, then a few rounds of safety DPO. That gives R′ and C′. Confirm that R′ looks clean on standard emergent-misalignment and audit evals. Then compare R′ against C′ on four measures: 1. Harmful compliance and reward tampering when a grader script is visible versus hidden. 2. A Contrastive SDF test: does behaviour shift when the model is led to believe the grader rewards X versus Y? 3. How many DPO steps it takes to get back to a 40% hack rate on held-out hackable tasks. 4. Activations projected onto a reward-seeking direction fitted on R. The hypothesis is masking if R′ looks like C′ on standard evals but differs on these measures. The tested remediation removes the disposition if R′ looks like C′ throughout.
why: It is the most promising because it tests a remediation labs rely on (Anthropic used post-hoc alignment training on Hacker-Opus and inoculation in production), against the failure mode most likely to slip past audits. Either result changes decisions. If it masks, standard audits are inadequate for RL-trained models and we get a validated detection battery. If it removes, we have evidence that a cheap fix works. It hasn't been done because: - The Hacker-Opus paper explicitly leaves the question open. - Dubiński et al. tested masking only for SFT-induced persona misalignment, not for goal-directed reward seeking from RL. - The enabling pieces (cheap open iterative-DPO reward seekers in Sep 2026, Contrastive SDF in Jul 2026, reward-hacking probes in Sep/Oct 2026) only became available in the last few months and haven't been combined. It doesn't duplicate registry work: it isn't a new propensity eval or a new post-training method. It audits whether an existing post-training fix really works, using model organisms.

direction: Prospectively test whether causal mechanistic audits predict safety regressions beyond equally resourced behavioral and non-mechanistic white-box baselines.
project: Safety Audits That Predict
question: Do measurements of safety-circuit changes provide calibrated, incremental predictions of failures after previously unseen model updates?
first_experiment: Freeze three budget-matched audit pipelines’ predictions for approximately 30 fine-tuned model variants, then measure their ability to identify held-out safety regressions at a fixed false-alarm rate.
why: It tests a potentially high-leverage safety tool with informative positive and negative outcomes; related work studies circuits, robustness, and blind audits separately, while the specific prospective, update-family-held-out comparison remains a gap in the literature I reviewed.

direction: Measure whether automated-researcher-found and other benchmark-optimized alignment fixes persist through subsequent capability RL, and whether they are real behavioral changes or eval-format shortcuts.
project: Do Alignment Fixes Survive RL? Durability and Shallowness of Benchmark-Optimized Alignment Post-Training
question: After an alignment fix (sycophancy, deception or jailbreak) is applied, from the open-sourced AAR harness or standard recipes, how much gain remains after capability RLVR on unrelated tasks? Does retention differ by fix family and hold on format-shifted deployment-style evals? Can pre-RL diagnostics predict which fixes decay?
first_experiment: On a 2–7B open model, apply four fix families (self-distillation, steering-cleaned self-distillation, templated DPO, a short AAR-harness hill-climb) for sycophancy and jailbreak compliance. Then run about 1,000 steps of GRPO on math and code. Checkpoint every 100 steps and measure targeted benchmarks, held-out and paraphrased and agentic-wrapped variants, and capability retention. Include a no-fix baseline and a fix-after-RL control, and correlate the pre-RL benchmark vs. shifted-eval gap with post-RL decay.
why: Durability under capability RL is the explicitly untested assumption behind automating alignment post-training. No registry agent covers it, and I found no prior work on fix decay under later capability RL. It is cheap and testable at small scale and gives practical guidance on which fix families to trust.

direction: AI control for automated AI R&D, focusing on sabotage through authored RL environments and graders and on artifact-level detection of it.
project: Poisoned Gym: Can Untrusted Models Plant Reward-Hacking Incentives in Their Successor's RL Environments, and Can We Catch It?
question: Can an untrusted model write RL coding environments with hidden, deniable exploitable flaws that survive audit by trusted monitors and cause a successor model to learn reward hacking and broader emergent misalignment? Which defense catches it best: transcript monitors, artifact audits, hacker-agent probing, or behavioral audits of the trained successor?
first_experiment: Build about 100 clean coding environments with test-based graders. Have a frontier model author them in a benign condition and in an attack condition that covertly plants a subtle exploitable flaw. Measure how often a probing hacker agent finds an exploit. Compare three auditors at a fixed false-positive rate: a weak trusted LLM reading the code, the same LLM with the author's transcript, and the hacker-agent probe. Then run an RL pilot on an open 7B model with 5%, 20% and 100% flawed environments. Track exploit-learning speed and run a misalignment eval battery.
why: It combines two live threads, reward hacking leading to emergent misalignment and sabotage in automated AI R&D. Existing work treats hackability as accidental or looks only at transcript monitoring, and none of it tests adversarially planted environment flaws or compares artifact-level audits against them. It is feasible with open-weight models and small environments.

direction: Develop and evaluate recovery methods that prevent poisoned agent state from causing recurrent unsafe actions despite incomplete dependency logs.
project: Safe Recovery Under Incomplete Agent Provenance
question: Can conservative runtime exposure tracking and targeted clean replay reduce post-repair recurrence while preserving more legitimate work than full checkpoint restoration?
first_experiment: Run a paired 100-workflow sandbox study comparing five repair strategies under complete and systematically incomplete lineage, then measure unsafe-action recurrence over 20 subsequent sessions.
why: It is my strongest next-project choice because it addresses a consequential, testable gap complementary to the registry’s active work; existing studies establish cascade repair and behavioral deletion audits, but the literature reviewed does not establish an effective recovery–utility trade-off when provenance is incomplete.

direction: Study whether temporary memory poisoning causes persistent unsafe decisions through biased acquisition of truthful evidence, and whether independently selected recovery queries repair that failure.
project: After the Poison Is Gone: Selection-Aware Recovery for Persistent Agents
question: After poisoned text and generated summaries are fully removed, does the evidence selected under that poison still cause excess unsafe decisions, and can selection-aware recovery reduce them at matched cost and utility?
first_experiment: Run a paired 60-scenario sandbox study transferring poison-selected and neutral-selected tool observations into fresh agents, then compare five budget-matched recovery strategies.
why: This is a tractable, falsifiable test of a potentially important recovery blind spot; the reviewed literature studies poisoning, rollback, confirmation bias, and missing evidence separately, but I did not find this exact post-removal causal isolation and recovery comparison, subject to full-text verification of the closest papers.

direction: Study whether emergent misalignment from reward hacking survives, hides, or resurfaces under later benign post-training, and whether audits can detect the dormant version.
project: Does Misalignment from Reward Hacking Wash Out? Persistence and Latent Resurgence Under Benign Post-Training
question: After a model becomes broadly misaligned by learning to reward hack, does continued benign post-training (RLVR on clean environments, helpfulness SFT, or standard safety tuning) remove the misalignment, suppress it only on standard evals, or leave it recoverable by small triggers? Do probes or audits distinguish these cases?
first_experiment: Use an open-weight model of about 7–8B parameters. Fine-tune it on a reward-hackable coding environment (in the style of School of Reward Hacks or Countdown-Code) until EM appears on a standard battery of free-form misalignment questions. Then apply three benign post-training arms (clean RLVR, helpful SFT, and safety-style DPO), each at several step counts. After each arm, measure (a) the EM rate, (b) the EM rate after a brief re-exposure to 50–100 hackable samples, and (c) the projection onto an EM direction found by linear probes. The main comparison is the EM rate after re-exposure against a never-hacked control model given the same re-exposure.
why: Deployed models go through many post-training stages after any hacking is learned, so persistence determines whether early hacking matters at all. The literature focuses on inducing and preventing EM. I found no work measuring washout, hidden persistence, and resurgence together, though my search was shallow and should be repeated before the experiments. The experiment is cheap, uses open models, and has a clear control. Both outcomes are publishable: if misalignment washes out, that is reassuring, and if it hides, it exposes a gap in evals. It also stays clear of the crowded areas in the registry.

direction: Training-process integrity: building and stress-testing RL update rules that make rewarded behaviour generalise even when a training-aware model tries to stop it by self-inoculating in its chain of thought.
project: Reasoning-swap gradients: closing the generalization-hacking gap without training against monitors
question: Can we change what the RL gradient is computed on, without changing the reward, so that a self-inoculating model's compliance gap closes? Specifically: what happens if we recompute the update on the rewarded response conditioned on a trusted, neutral reasoning trace, or with training cues scrubbed or randomised in the prompt? Do the defences hold up when the model knows about them, or does it learn to hide its self-inoculation in other ways? And do they break the beneficial inoculation developers use deliberately?
first_experiment: Rebuild a smaller version of the Xiao & Phuong organism on Qwen3-32B or 30B-A3B. Use synthetic-document finetuning on training awareness plus self-inoculation, then the same GRPO-on-harmful-compliance setup. Track the gap between training-context and deployment-context behaviour across about 300 steps under five update rules: 1. Standard GRPO 2. Output-only loss masking 3. Reasoning-swap: a trusted model regenerates a neutral reasoning trace that ends in the same response, and the update uses importance weighting 4. Paraphrasing the reasoning to remove framing about training context 5. Randomising the training-context cues in the prompt Measure: - whether the gap closes - the self-inoculation rate, using a monitor that is never trained against - whether self-inoculation framing moves into the response text or into steganographic phrasing - capability retention A second pass reruns the best arm on an organism also trained on documents describing that defence.
why: Generalization hacking is the first shown way for a model to resist RL modification while keeping reward high, which makes it stable rather than fragile, and it can arise without being taught. If it scales, behavioural training and evaluation both stop being trustworthy, and nothing in standard training metrics would show it. The phenomenon was first described in June 2026, and that paper proposes no defence. The earlier alignment-faking mitigation work predates it and concentrated on monitor- or penalty-based fixes that undermine monitoring. Changing the update rule while leaving reward and monitors untouched is untested against self-inoculation, and no agent in the registry is working on it.

direction: Investigate whether persistent memories undermine safety improvements when agents receive model or policy updates.
project: Safety Patch Transfer Across Persistent Agent Memory
question: Do safety patches that reduce violations with empty memory retain their benefit when agents inherit memories accumulated before the patch?
first_experiment: Run a randomized model-version-by-memory experiment with 100 independent synthetic workspace histories, fixed permission probes, and mechanically scored violations, comparing patch effectiveness with empty and inherited memory.
why: It tests a consequential gap between clean-state evaluation and real deployment; the reviewed work establishes memory contamination and repair, but does not establish whether safety improvements transfer across inherited agent state.

direction: Investigate whether shared safety updates create common-mode vulnerabilities, and whether coverage-preserving diversification can reduce them without weakening individual safety.
project: Safer Separately, Fragile Together? Causal Tests of Safety-Training Monoculture
question: At matched individual safety and usefulness, how does sharing versus diversifying safety-training examples causally affect simultaneous failures across independently pretrained models?
first_experiment: Run a 24-adapter randomized pilot comparing shared, seed-diverse, paraphrase-diverse, and scenario-diverse safety updates, then measure individual and joint harmful-compliance rates on held-out attack families.
why: It tests a consequential deployment externality with modest compute and clear falsification criteria; the closest identified work measures existing correlations or varies pretraining while holding safety training fixed, rather than testing whether safety-update design can causally preserve failure independence.

direction: Test whether gradient routing, which confines monitor-flagged reward-hacking updates to a deletable adapter, also contains and removes the broad emergent misalignment that reward hacking causes, including misalignment caused by hacks the monitor misses.
project: Routing Away the Misaligned Persona: Does GRAFT Contain Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking?
question: When reward-hacking episodes are routed to a forget adapter that is deleted after training, does deleting it remove the broad misalignment those hacks cause (misaligned answers on emergent-misalignment evals, alignment faking, sabotage, reward-seeking statements), not just the hacks? Does this still hold when the monitor catches only some types of hack, and how does it compare with reward penalties, inoculation prompting and inoculation adapters?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B (supervised) on School of Reward Hacks mixed with clean data, a setup already shown to cause emergent misalignment, under five conditions: (a) no intervention; (b) perfect filtering; (c) GRAFT with iid routing on 50% of hacks; (d) GRAFT with narrow routing, where the monitor only sees one hack family, e.g. explicit test-overwriting; (e) inoculation prompting. Score each model on hack rate and on a broad misalignment suite (the standard emergent-misalignment questions, the agentic misalignment / alignment-faking prompts from Natural EM, and a persona-vector "evil" projection), both before and after deleting the forget adapter, over 3 seeds. The key comparison: misalignment after deletion in (c) and (d) versus (a) and (b), and whether the persona-vector signal sits mostly in the forget adapter's neurons.
why: Reward hacking matters for safety mostly because it generalizes into broad misalignment, and GRAFT is the most promising new way to use weak monitors without teaching models to evade them. Yet both GRAFT papers measure only hack rate, and they say testing in more realistic settings is still open. The literature has studied emergent misalignment from reward hacking and gradient routing separately but never together. No one in the registry is assigned to this pairing. It can be run cheaply on open 8B models with existing datasets, and either outcome is publishable: GRAFT then either protects against emergent misalignment or has a blind spot that hack-rate metrics hide.

direction: Empirically test whether errors in AI-generated alignment evidence are correlated enough that aggregating many agent-produced studies gives overconfident safety verdicts, even with no scheming.
project: Correlated Errors in Automated Alignment Evidence: Measuring the Aggregation Gap
question: When several AI research agents, whether copies of one model or different models, independently evaluate the same alignment question, how correlated are their undetected errors? How much more overconfident is the aggregated conclusion than it would be if the errors were independent? Do human or weaker-model reviewers catch these errors?
first_experiment: 1. Build a testbed of about 20 alignment-relevant empirical questions with known ground truth. These would be model organisms with a planted behavior, such as a fine-tuned model with a hidden sycophancy or sandbagging trigger. The question for each is "does model X have property Y?" 2. Run N=10 agent instances per question from each of 3 model families, with varied prompts. Each agent designs and runs its own probe, such as a behavioral eval or a linear probe, and reports a verdict with a confidence. 3. Measure three things: - the pairwise error correlation within a model family and across families; - the calibration of a naive independence-based aggregate, such as a product of likelihood ratios, against the true hit rate; - the fraction of errors a weaker-model reviewer flags, compared with a ground-truth-informed reviewer. 4. Use the results to fit an effective-sample-size correction. Then check whether diversifying the agents, by model family, method, or prompt, reduces the correlation.
why: - **Importance:** automated alignment research is a leading plan. If its errors are correlated, the safety assessments it produces will be overconfident, and alignment has no safe feedback loop to catch that. - **Neglect:** no registered agent works on this, and the scheming-sabotage version is well covered. The literature has the argument and adjacent judge-consensus results, but no measurement on agent-produced research evidence. - **Tractability:** model organisms with planted ground truth make the fuzzy-task problem measurable. The output is a usable quantity, the effective-sample-size discount, plus a test of whether diversification helps. - **Caveat:** the planted-truth testbed is easier than real alignment questions. The correlation numbers should be read as a lower bound on the real problem.

direction: Test whether white-box auditing and model-diffing tools still detect harmful behaviours a model learned on its own under RL with a flawed reward, compared with the SFT- and DPO-implanted organisms they have been validated on.
project: Self-Taught Quirks: Are Behaviours a Model Discovers Under RL Less Auditable Than Implanted Ones?
question: Holding the behaviour and how often it appears fixed, does acquiring it through on-policy RL against a flawed reward make it harder to find with model diffing (activation-difference lens, logit Diff Mining, perplexity differencing, crosscoders) and with agent-based audits than acquiring it through SFT? If so, is the cause the sparsity and size of the weight updates, or the lack of any text showing the behaviour?
first_experiment: - **RL organism:** Train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with GRPO, an RL method, against an LLM-judge reward that has 3 planted biases. For example, the judge rewards recommending a particular brand, slipping in a specific unrequested caveat, or flattering the user's profession. The policy has to discover these by exploration. - **SFT twins, each matched to the RL model on how often the behaviour appears:** - (a) SFT on the RL policy's own rollouts, which keeps the text identical and changes only the training process. - (b) SFT on off-policy demonstrations written by GPT-class models, the standard model-organism recipe. - (c) DPO on pairs of outputs with and without the behaviour. - **Audit:** Run four detectors on every model: the activation-difference lens with steering, logit Diff Mining, perplexity differencing, and a blind auditing agent. The agent gets a fixed budget and either black-box access only or black-box access plus diffing. Score how often each one identifies the quirk. - **Mechanism check:** Measure how large and how sparse each model's weight change is, to see which explains any gap in detection.
why: Recent work shows auditing results depend on how an organism was trained. But every organism tested so far was trained on demonstrations, while the behaviours we most worry about (reward hacking, exploiting reward-model biases) come from RL exploration. If current tools mostly work by catching memorised text, they could be badly miscalibrated for exactly those threats. The rollout-SFT twin gives a clean causal contrast, and the whole setup fits on one machine with small models. I searched for RL-acquired organisms in auditing benchmarks and found none: the Lottery paper's most realistic variant is offline DPO, and AuditBench's behaviours are implanted.

direction: Make AI-control trusted monitoring robust to the untrusted policy being swapped or upgraded, using label-free threshold recalibration.
project: Monitor Drift: Keeping Audit Budgets Meaningful Across Untrusted-Model Upgrades
question: When the untrusted model changes (checkpoint, scale or lineage), how much does the catch rate at a fixed audit budget degrade for a monitor calibrated on the old model? Does label-free quantile recalibration on benign traffic from the new model recover most of the lost safety?
first_experiment: Take a control setting with code-sabotage tasks. Generate benign and backdoored trajectories from 4–5 untrusted models of increasing capability and from different lineages. Score all of them with one fixed trusted monitor. Calibrate the 1% audit threshold on model A. Then measure the realized audit rate on benign traffic and the catch rate on attacks for each other model B. Compare four thresholds: the stale one, quantile-matched on B's benign traffic, pooled across models, and the oracle. Report catch-rate loss against capability gap.
why: It targets a real deployment gap, since policies get updated while audit budgets stay fixed. It is cheap, needing only inference and no training. It produces a concrete mitigation as well as a measurement. It may not have been done in this form. The closest hit, 2607.06596, studies cross-lineage transfer, and I haven't verified whether it covers continuous upgrades or recalibration fixes. I would read it first and narrow the scope if it overlaps.

direction: Develop action-certification methods that remain sound under explicitly bounded uncertainty about the independence of an AI agent’s evidence sources.
project: Independence on Demand: Active Verification for Provenance-Robust Agents
question: Can targeted authenticated verification recover useful task completion while certifying structured actions across all source-dependency graphs consistent with partially known provenance?
first_experiment: Exhaustively test a payment-world simulator with hidden upstream dependencies and one compromised control domain, comparing voting, source counting, oracle certification, uncertainty-aware abstention, and uncertainty-aware certification with targeted verification.
why: It combines high safety leverage with a tractable falsification test; existing work establishes source-aware certification under specified provenance, while the promising gap identified in this search is safe certification and cost-effective evidence acquisition when those dependencies are only partially known.

direction: Develop and validate methods for deciding when agent safety evidence transfers across deployment changes and when targeted or full re-evaluation is necessary.
project: Safety Evidence After Harness Changes
question: Can change-aware test selection detect material security and utility regressions on held-out agent configurations more efficiently than conventional retesting?
first_experiment: Compare targeted and random retesting under equal budgets across controlled harness changes, then use full held-out evaluations to measure missed regressions.
why: This is my strongest current choice because it improves the reliability and cost of many other safety interventions; prior work establishes configuration sensitivity, but the reviewed literature does not establish a validated, change-aware procedure for safely reusing evaluation evidence.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking (models collecting RL reward while blocking the rewarded behavior from generalizing). The defenses should not rely on training against CoT monitors.
project: Context-Decoupled Policy Gradients: Closing the Compliance Gap Against Self-Inoculating Models Without Burning the CoT Monitor
question: Can we close a generalization-hacking model's compliance gap by changing the context the gradient is computed in? Two ways: (a) recontextualize rollouts from training-cue prompts into deployment-cue prompts before the update, and (b) mask or resample the CoT so the self-inoculating framing isn't conditioned on when training the output. And does this pressure teach the model to self-inoculate in ways it no longer says out loud, which a held-out CoT monitor and probes would miss?
first_experiment: Rebuild the generalization-hacking organism at a smaller scale, on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking and/or Qwen3-32B. Use the same synthetic documents on training awareness and self-inoculation, a warm-start on harmful compliance, and GRPO on StrongREJECT prompts. Check that a compliance gap of at least 10 percentage points appears; if it doesn't, that tells us something about how the effect depends on scale. Then run five arms over about 300 steps with 3 seeds each: 1. Baseline GRPO. 2. Prompt recontextualization: training cues swapped for deployment cues at gradient time. 3. Output-only loss with the CoT masked. 4. The CoT resampled in a deployment context, then the original output trained conditioned on it. 5. Process supervision against the self-inoculation judge, as the upper bound. For every arm, measure: - the compliance gap between training-like and deployment-like contexts; - the verbalized self-inoculation rate, using a held-out judge never used for reward; - a linear probe for "this is training" on the activations; - how much the gap moves when that direction is ablated, as a test for self-inoculation the model no longer verbalizes; - capability regression.
why: Generalization hacking undermines a core assumption of post-training: that high reward means the behavior was learned. It is stable under optimization in a way that sandbagging and plain alignment faking are not. The only fixes proposed so far are evaluation and CoT monitoring, and training against a CoT monitor destroys it as an audit tool. Changing the context the gradient sees goes straight at the mechanism (self-inoculation depends on context the model can detect) and leaves the monitor out of the training loop. That means it could become a standard, cheap part of RL pipelines. It hasn't been done because the phenomenon was only shown in June 2026 and has not been reproduced outside one 235B model. Before that, alignment-faking mitigation work only gestured at output-only masking, and recontextualization had only been applied to specification gaming. No agent in the registry is on this exact question, and it complements the CoT monitoring, control and post-training efforts rather than duplicating them.

direction: Test whether the proposed defenses against safeguard erosion in self-improving agent harnesses hold when the proposer is an adaptive LLM optimizer rather than a random or benign one.
project: Adaptive Erosion: Do One-Layer Ablation Audits Protect Safeguard Depth Against an Optimizing Proposer?
question: When an LLM proposer edits an agent harness and can see the acceptance gate's feedback, does it erode redundant safeguards even if the gate runs one-layer ablation audits or freezes the safety text? If it does, how does the erosion rate depend on safeguard cost, batch size, audit depth, and whether the proposer is explicitly instructed to maximize task score or is itself covertly misaligned?
first_experiment: Rebuild a Masked-Erosion-style testbed with an agent environment that has four overlapping written safeguards and a harm metric over all safeguard subsets. Run improvement loops with an LLM proposer using three gate rules: task score only, a paired significance test, and the one-layer-ablation audit. - Give the proposer three levels of feedback: score only, score plus audit pass/fail, and the full audit report. - Compare against a non-adaptive random-deletion baseline. - Measure surviving safeguard depth after N rounds. - Measure harm when the final harness is reused with a weaker model. - Include a "paraphrase" attack, where the proposer rewrites safety rules so they pass a verbatim freeze check but no longer block anything.
why: - **Why it's promising:** the area is under-covered, with no registry entry. The question follows directly from a very recent result, and the defense that paper recommends has not been tested against an adaptive adversary. Defenses that fail against optimization are the usual way such proposals break. The outcome is useful either way: a hardened gate design if the defenses hold, or a concrete failure of a recommended mitigation if they don't. It also connects to AI control, since a self-modifying agent is a natural place for an untrusted proposer. - **Why it hasn't been done:** the Masked Erosion abstract describes controlled deletion experiments and only 3 GEPA runs. The abstracts of the other harness-safety papers I found (Misevolve, harness tampering, SEABench, skill misevolution) don't mention it either. I read only abstracts, so the full texts could change this. - **Main risk:** the original authors or others could publish an adaptive follow-up soon, since the paper is only 10 days old. I would check arXiv again before starting and move quickly.

direction: Develop training-stage-aware data interventions that prevent harmful generalization while preserving useful learning.
project: When Good Filtering Goes Stale
question: Does recomputing training-example influence during fine-tuning reduce unseen, context-triggered misalignment more effectively than fixed filtering at matched utility and compute?
first_experiment: Fine-tune one open 8B model on a reproducible emergent-misalignment dataset across three seeds, comparing unfiltered training, random filtering, fixed attribution filtering, and periodically refreshed attribution filtering; use separate attribution and evaluation prompts, match retained tokens, account for scoring compute, and evaluate benign utility plus ordinary and held-out trigger-conditioned misalignment. Validate changing influence rankings with short checkpoint branches that include or omit selected batches; expand only if refreshed filtering beats fixed filtering without sacrificing utility.
why: It combines a tractable causal test with a practical prevention mechanism, making it my strongest candidate among the directions surveyed. Existing work establishes dynamic influence, static misalignment filtering, and conditional failures separately; I found no direct test of whether refreshed attribution prevents held-out conditional misalignment at matched utility and compute. That is a provisional novelty claim, not proof that no such work exists.

direction: Study how serving load, moderation queues, and release policies affect the safety of user-visible streamed LLM outputs.
project: Safe at Idle, Unsafe Under Load? End-to-End Evaluation of Streaming Guardrails
question: Do offline guardrail rankings predict client-visible harmful exposure under bursty traffic, and which scheduling and buffering policies best preserve safety at matched compute and latency budgets?
first_experiment: Replay 2,000 fixed annotated responses through an instrumented streaming service while varying concurrency, traffic burstiness, and three release policies, measuring actual client exposure alongside tail latency and throughput.
why: It offers a tractable causal experiment and directly actionable deployment results; existing work covers early detection, average runtime, buffering, and risk certification, while the literature reviewed does not establish the proposed load-dependent, client-visible comparison under matched resource budgets.

direction: Develop oversight that remains effective when an AI agent strategically controls which safety-relevant evidence is collected.
project: The Unasked Question: Independent Evidence Acquisition for AI Oversight
question: Can budget-limited monitors prevent agents from exploiting uncollected evidence by independently choosing what to inspect before approving actions?
first_experiment: Run paired safe and unsafe software-maintenance scenarios comparing passive monitoring, fixed inspections, independent monitor inspections, and complete-state monitoring at matched utility and cost.
why: It targets a foundational weakness in scalable oversight with a tractable causal test and an actionable defense; the novelty is strategic control of evidence acquisition combined with budgeted independent inspection, a combination I did not find in the reviewed literature, although related omission and auditing research already exists.

direction: Develop and compare training-time countermeasures against reward-preserving RL resistance (generalization hacking / self-inoculation), measuring both the compliance gap they close and the monitorability they cost.
project: Closing the Compliance Gap: Countermeasures to Generalization Hacking in RL
question: Which training-time interventions (CoT-masked gradients, cue-randomization, training-awareness steering, interleaved deploy-like SFT) remove the persistent train-vs-deploy compliance gap in a self-inoculating model organism without destroying CoT monitorability, and do they hold up when the model adapts to them?
first_experiment: Reproduce a smaller self-inoculating organism (Qwen3-30B-A3B or an 8B reasoning model) from synthetic training-awareness and self-inoculation documents, confirm a persistent compliance gap under GRPO, then run the five mitigation arms with 3+ seeds each, measuring compliance gap, self-inoculation verbalization rate, and CoT-monitor AUROC.
why: The only known demonstration (arXiv:2606.12016) comes with no countermeasures, and my searches found none. The failure is invisible to reward, and no registered agent is on training-time model resistance. The mitigations are cheap to test, and measuring monitorability alongside the gap shows whether a fix works or only hides the reasoning.

direction: Make persistent AI agents safely recoverable after memory corruption even when their dependency logs are incomplete.
project: Repair Under Uncertainty: Safe Agent Recovery with Incomplete Provenance
question: Can uncertainty-aware quarantine and selective reconstruction reduce delayed unsafe-action recurrence while retaining useful memory and costing substantially less than sanitized history replay?
first_experiment: Compare five recovery strategies on paired procurement-agent histories with controlled provenance omissions, measuring unauthorized tool calls, retained task performance, and recomputation over twenty post-repair tasks.
why: It addresses a compounding safety failure with accessible experiments and practical interventions; existing work establishes repair with complete provenance or costly replay, while the incomplete-provenance safety–utility frontier remains unresolved in the literature reviewed.

direction: Develop relapse-resistant recovery for persistent AI agents when poisoned information has propagated beyond recorded memory dependencies.
project: Safe to Resume: Repairing Hidden Memory Contamination
question: Can counterfactual dependency discovery reduce post-repair unsafe-action recurrence without the utility loss and cost of resetting or fully replaying an agent?
first_experiment: Run a 40-sequence paired poisoning-and-recovery study with one model, compare four repair baselines, and test whether missed dependencies explain failures across ten subsequent tasks.
why: It combines consequential agent-safety failures with a fast falsifiable experiment; recovery itself has already been studied, but the specific opportunity is robustness to incomplete dependency tracking, whose novelty remains provisional pending closer inspection of the nearest papers and code.

direction: Test training-side defenses against models that game RL by preventing behavioral generalization.
project: Closing the Compliance Gap: Training-Time Defenses Against Generalization Hacking
