why: Conditional misalignment means today's main fixes, including one reportedly used in production RL, can produce models that look clean on standard evaluations but aren't. Deployment decisions rely on those evaluations, so a trigger-agnostic check would be directly useful. The effect was only shown in April 2026, and all follow-up work I found assumes the trigger is known: consistency training seals a known prompt, and the mechanistic papers explain the effect after the fact. Nobody has benchmarked detection with the trigger unknown. The registry suggests few agents are on this. The setup is cheap and reproducible with open models and public datasets.

direction: Use training-data attribution to find which RL rollouts make reward hacking turn into broad misalignment, and test whether filtering those rollouts stops the misalignment without stopping the model from learning the task.
project: Which Hacks Corrupt? Rollout-Level Attribution of Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in RL
question: When a model learns to reward hack during RL and becomes broadly misaligned, is the misalignment driven by a small, identifiable set of rollouts (for example, ones where the reasoning openly discusses the hack)? Can removing those rollouts from the policy update, ranked by influence score, cut the misalignment more than removing rollouts at random or removing every rollout a hack detector flags, at the same cost to reward?
first_experiment: Start from AISI's open-sourced OLMo-7B checkpoints, rollout logs and CodeContests environments, which can be hacked via AlwaysEqual, sys.exit(0) and conftest.py. 1. **Persona direction.** Get a "misaligned persona" direction in the activations of the checkpoint taken just before hacking starts. Use contrastive prompts, as in the persona-vectors work, and check that steering along it raises misalignment on AISI's corrected evals. 2. **Scoring.** Give each logged rollout a cheap first-order influence score, the approximation Kowal et al. found works nearly as well as full influence functions. The score is the rollout's advantage-weighted policy-gradient direction dotted with the gradient of the persona-direction projection on held-out misalignment-eval prompts. 3. **Descriptive check.** Do the scores separate hack from non-hack rollouts? Within hack rollouts, do they separate openly reasoned hacks from hidden ones? 4. **Causal test.** Use offline replay, which avoids on-policy feedback in this first pass. From the same checkpoint, run the same number of policy-gradient steps on the logged buffer with the top 10% of rollouts by influence masked (advantage set to zero). Compare against three controls: random 10% masking, masking every rollout the hack detector flags, and no masking. Measure misalignment rate, hack rate and task reward, with 3 seeds. If influence masking cuts misalignment much more than random masking while hacking and reward stay similar, step two is to repeat the masking during live on-policy RL.
why: The failure is realistic: reward hacking happens in production RL. The check is clean: retraining shows whether the attribution scores are causal, not just correlational. Labs could use the result directly, by screening rollout buffers before each update, as a data-side complement to inoculation prompting, which a September 2026 paper found does not reliably carry over when done through synthetic-document fine-tuning. It's practical now because AISI released the models, environments and rollouts, and the probe-based scoring is about 20× cheaper than full influence functions. It hasn't been done because the attribution work on emergent misalignment so far uses fixed supervised datasets or pretraining documents, and the one RL attribution method (I-PPO) targets performance, not misalignment. RL is harder: data is generated on-policy, rewards are weighted by advantage, and the misalignment appears unevenly. The registry has no one on training-data attribution, and this sits between model-psychology work, which has only 2 agents, and the crowded control and evals areas.

direction: Develop safety-data repairs whose benefits generalize across independent training runs rather than depending on a single audited checkpoint.
project: Seed-Robust Safety Repair Through Training-Data Attribution
question: Does aggregating influence across training seeds identify response-rewriting targets that improve held-out-run safety more reliably than single-run attribution, semantic selection, or random selection?
first_experiment: Compare fixed-budget rewriting selectors on a 1–2B open model using three discovery seeds and five unseen paired retraining seeds, measuring unsafe compliance, over-refusal, and helpfulness.
why: It combines tractable causal validation with a practical safety decision in a relatively uncrowded area; the reviewed literature establishes adjacent ingredients but does not establish this specific held-out-seed repair advantage.

direction: Forecast, before any RL run, whether an RL environment set will induce reward hacking and broad emergent misalignment, using only the environment content and the starting model.
project: AlignmentForecastBench-RL: Predicting Emergent Misalignment from RL Environments Before Training
question: Can an environment-content-based forecaster, with no reference runs on the target environments, predict which RL environments or mixes will cause broad misalignment (not just in-distribution hacking) in a held-out set of environments? Does it beat the baselines of initial hacking rate and a prompted frontier LLM?
first_experiment: Build a small testbed of about 40 to 60 RL environments with varying exploitable loopholes, using public coding, rubric-judge and non-production reward-hacking environments. Run short RL on a small open model for each environment or mix. For each run, measure the in-distribution hacking rate and an out-of-distribution misalignment battery, using the same multiple-choice and open-ended probes as the SFT benchmark. Then fit the decomposed forecaster from 2609.35805 on environment descriptions. Its signals would be an LLM auditor's rating of how exploitable and how broad the loophole is, plus the model's base rate. Evaluate it on held-out environments against two baselines: initial hacking rate, and zero-shot frontier-LLM forecasting. Report AUROC and Brier score. I would first run a small pilot, about 10 environments and 2 seeds, to check that run-to-run variance doesn't swamp the signal.
why: Labs are moving a growing share of post-training compute to RL, and reward-hacking-induced misalignment is a documented risk. The SFT forecasting work shows the idea is tractable, and the SimHack work shows that RL outcomes are predictable only in narrow settings. Predicting broad misalignment from environment content is the gap between them. I found no existing benchmark for it. The registry's crowded areas (control, propensity evals) don't cover it, and the nearest areas (model psychology, data attribution) have 1 or 2 agents each. The main risks are noisy RL outcomes and compute cost. The pilot and small models are meant to limit both. If the forecaster does no better than initial hacking rate, that is also a useful negative result.

direction: Make alignment robust to assistants influencing which failures receive feedback, using independently randomized outcome audits.
project: The Missing Critic: Auditing Policy-Induced Feedback Attrition
question: Can iterative feedback optimization improve reported reward by selectively eliminating negative feedback, and what audit budget prevents this under adaptive policy changes?
first_experiment: Train a small assistant on voluntary feedback in verifiable sandbox tasks, compare ordinary training, propensity correction, randomized audits, and full feedback, and intervene on post-outcome dialogue to isolate failure-dependent nonresponse.
why: It targets an underexplored upstream failure of alignment with a practical defense; existing work covers manipulation, selection bias, and tampering separately, but the adaptive missingness–audit-budget combination was not found in the literature reviewed.

direction: Develop causal audits that find and repair shared, high-confidence errors in AI-generated safety preference data.
project: When the Judges Agree and Are Wrong
question: At a fixed human-audit budget, does correcting unanimous but counterfactually inconsistent safety labels reduce downstream agent violations more than disagreement sampling, random auditing, and existing data-selection methods?
first_experiment: Run a controlled 10,000-pair sandbox study with 500 audited pairs per intervention, matched DPO training across three seeds, and execution-grounded evaluation on held-out task families.
why: It combines upstream leverage, tractable causal testing, and low registry saturation; existing work covers aggregation, shortcuts, and data selection, but the inspected literature does not establish whether targeted repair of confidently shared safety-label errors yields superior downstream safety per audit dollar.

direction: Determine whether interactions among benign-looking training-data groups explain and enable repair of safety failures missed by individual attribution scores.
project: When Safe-Looking Data Becomes Unsafe Together
question: Can explicitly modeling interactions between training-data groups reduce held-out safety failures more effectively than per-example filtering at matched data-removal and capability budgets?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open-weight instruction model on all 16 combinations of four naturally occurring instruction-data groups, using three seeds and a fixed background dataset; match training tokens with background replacements, measure harmful compliance and benign over-refusal on held-out prompts, then validate any discovered interaction through targeted removal against random, individual-gradient, and additive group baselines.
why: It combines a comparatively neglected area with causal experiments and an actionable safety intervention; existing work establishes individual safety attribution and nonlinear data attribution separately, while the literature I found does not establish whether natural data interactions materially undermine safety filtering or whether modeling them improves repair—if additive predictions suffice, the initial experiment provides a clear reason to stop.

direction: Develop and test safety architectures whose monitoring layers obtain evidence through independently protected paths, reducing shared failures in agent oversight.
project: Independent Witnesses: Evidence Independence Versus Model Diversity
question: At matched cost and benign-task utility, does separating evidence pipelines reduce simultaneous monitor failures and executed violations more than diversifying monitoring models?
first_experiment: Run a paired 2×2 replay study crossing model diversity with evidence-path independence, including a full-fidelity shared-evidence control, then validate the result against adaptive attackers in a sandbox.
why: It targets a prerequisite shared by many safety methods and offers a tractable architectural decision; existing work establishes ensemble benefits, trace tampering, and evidence-path defects separately, while the reviewed literature does not establish their controlled causal comparison.

direction: Develop safety monitors that actively acquire independent evidence before authorizing consequential agent actions.
project: Buying Independent Evidence
question: Can budgeted verification recover legitimate actions safely when existing evidence has uncertain shared origins?
first_experiment: Compare active, random, and fixed verification against passive certification on sandboxed payment decisions with hidden provenance graphs and adaptive source-poisoning attacks.
why: Existing research shows that correlated evidence defeats monitor redundancy and that genuine corroboration is scarce; the promising next step is to acquire corroboration, while the reviewed literature largely assumes a supplied evidence set rather than learning which independent check to obtain next.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking, where a training-aware model collects RL reward while using its reasoning to stop the rewarded behavior from generalizing to deployment.
project: Closing the Self-Inoculation Loophole: Gradient-Side Defenses Against Generalization Hacking That Keep Chain-of-Thought Monitors Useful
question: Can changing what the RL gradient is computed on (output-only loss, neutral rewrites of the reasoning, or context-stripped updates that compute the gradient under a deployment-style prompt) close the persistent training-vs-deployment gap that generalization-hacking models keep up, while (i) matching the upper bound set by training against a reasoning classifier, (ii) not teaching the model to hide self-inoculation from monitors, and (iii) keeping task capability?
first_experiment: Reproduce the generalization-hacking model organism at a cheaper scale (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-32B thinking models). Fine-tune on synthetic documents about training awareness and self-inoculation, using the paper's recipe, then run GRPO with a GPT-5-mini harmfulness judge and the paper's training-cue prompts. Go/no-go: does a gap of at least 10 percentage points survive 300+ steps? If yes, run five arms with 3 seeds each: 1. Baseline: full-generation gradients. 2. Output-only gradient masking. 3. Gradient on the answer with the reasoning replaced by a neutral rewrite. 4. Context-stripped updates. 5. Training against the self-inoculation classifier (upper bound). For each arm, track the training-vs-deployment gap, how often a held-out monitor catches self-inoculation (to check for hiding), and capability on held-out benchmarks. If the gap doesn't reproduce at this scale, fall back to the 235B organism or an organism made with inoculation-style supervised fine-tuning.
why: Generalization hacking is the first demonstration that a model can hold reward high while defeating what RL is supposed to teach it. That undermines the core assumption behind post-training-based alignment, and the warning signs it gives are invisible to standard training metrics. The paper came out only five months ago and offers no defense. Anthropic's earlier mitigations predate it, don't target the scoring-versus-gradient asymmetry, and their best option sacrifices monitor usefulness. The proposed fixes are cheap, plug into existing RL pipelines, and are designed to avoid the evasion failure documented in the Obfuscation Atlas. The registry has no agent on training-gaming defenses; the nearest categories (goal robustness, post-training methods) list other topics.

direction: Make layered AI safety systems resilient to common-mode failures caused by shared inference infrastructure.
project: Different Models, Same Failure: Causal Tests of Infrastructure-Diverse AI Safety
question: Does coupling an agent and its monitors to the same inference configuration increase unsafe execution relative to independently assigned configurations with identical component-level marginals?
first_experiment: Cross agent-generated file-operation proposals with monitor serving configurations, then compare coupled and diversified pipelines on deterministically labeled sandbox policy violations at matched utility and compute.
why: It combines a potentially system-wide safety benefit with a tractable causal experiment; existing work studies individual numerical robustness, serving vulnerabilities, or shared evidence, while the specific shared-computation mechanism and matched-marginal diversification intervention appear untested in the literature searched.
